Chapter library

Recent simulation redesign

Ten chapters · 251 distinct models · 1,802 stored checkpoints. Revision of existing learning tools; chapter approval is a separate step.

How to study one operation

  1. Use Next to replay one operation. Read the operation and its reason beside the drawing.
  2. Use Before or Compare to inspect the preceding and current exact states. The first displayed checkpoint has no preceding state.
  3. Pause the movement or adjust Transition to inspect geometry in transit. Labels and counters describe the target checkpoint; interpolated geometry does not assert fractional algorithm steps or intermediate arithmetic results.
  4. Open Exact changes for the complete changed fields, or Full exact state for the underlying stored values. Rounded readouts carry an approximation sign.
  5. Use Browse all operations to jump directly to any recorded operation. Original overview preserves the preceding domain diagram as an additional view.
  6. Every model starts paused. Arrow keys navigate checkpoints, Home/End select endpoints and Space controls playback when the model itself has focus. Reduced-motion mode preserves the exact states without animated transitions.

What was redesigned

Record regions and moving cuts; byte addresses and read/write heads; suspended recursive continuations and connected invocation trees; probability masses on fixed axes; density areas and individual residual contributions; matrix operations and their companion matrices; conditional beliefs separated from evidence; and graph searches with complete path-aware frontier records.

For geometry that already represents the concept correctly, its coordinates and topology are retained. Its player, explanation, comparison, changed-object emphasis and replay are rebuilt. This is not a claim that every original drawing was discarded.

Verification

Every stored model and checkpoint passed browser checks for rendering, explanation, checkpoint selection, label containment and preservation of scientific records. All ten editable laboratories passed valid input, rejected-input preservation and replacement without accumulating hidden players. Pause and resume, manual transition progress, reduced motion, keyboard-compatible controls, print checkpoint generation, mobile containment and enlarged text were checked. Lessons, questions, final rules, source references and scientific engines remain unchanged. The graph laboratory's literal input was corrected after mathematical markup was found inside its textarea.

Expectation, Linearity, Indicators, and Moments · 19 models
  • Signed mean: accumulate value times probability

  • Absolute mean: remove sign before multiplying

    Each contribution is transformed value times probability. Negative and positive contributions accumulate with their signs.

  • Heavy tail: probability shrinks, mean contribution stays constant

    A finite prefix cannot prove an infinite expectation exists. Track positive, negative and absolute contributions separately.

  • Symmetric truncation: zero signed prefix, divergent absolute prefix

    A finite prefix cannot prove an infinite expectation exists. Track positive, negative and absolute contributions separately.

  • LOTUS: square each value before averaging

    Each contribution is transformed value times probability. Negative and positive contributions accumulate with their signs.

  • Many-to-one square: each original mass contributes once

    Each contribution is transformed value times probability. Negative and positive contributions accumulate with their signs.

  • Linearity works on the same outcome; products retain dependence

    Compute the expression inside each outcome before averaging. Linearity does not require independence.

  • Fixed points: a permutation realization and its indicator probabilities

    One diagram is one permutation; the expected count averages indicators over all uniform permutations.

  • Running minimum: tests, successful updates, and record probabilities

    Distinguish a realized record update from its probability. At position i, symmetry gives the record probability.

  • Occupancy: sample placements versus mean occupied bins

    A new ball may create a new occupied bin or a collision. Realized counts and expected counts are different quantities.

  • Occupancy: sample placements versus mean occupied bins

    A new ball may create a new occupied bin or a collision. Realized counts and expected counts are different quantities.

  • Layer cake: one level for every reached integer threshold

    An outcome contributes one horizontal layer for each attained threshold. Tail probabilities recover moments by weighted sums.

  • Squared heights: odd increments weight each survival layer

    An outcome contributes one horizontal layer for each attained threshold. Tail probabilities recover moments by weighted sums.

  • Capped trials: surviving paths execute the next trial

    The kth trial runs only if earlier trials failed. Sum execution probabilities, not stopping-time masses.

  • Central moment: square the distance from the fixed mean

    Each contribution is transformed value times probability. Negative and positive contributions accumulate with their signs.

  • Squared-loss prediction: move a constant on a fixed parabola

    Separate irreducible variance from the squared displacement of the proposed constant from the mean.

  • Threshold payoff: transform before averaging

    Each contribution is transformed value times probability. Negative and positive contributions accumulate with their signs.

  • Graph indicators: a selected edge or triangle uses specific vertices

    Edge and triangle indicators have different event requirements. Shared edges do not prevent linearity of expectation.

  • Overlapping windows: slide the start, preserve bit identities

    Count every eligible window, including overlapping ones. Dependence between windows does not invalidate summing expectations.

    The normal component reverses while tangential components remain. Connect this geometric action to determinant sign.

Intelligent Agents, Rationality, Task Environments, and Problem Formulation · 17 models
  • Percept, internal update, action and next state

    Follow environment, percept, internal decision and action in causal order. A percept is not automatically the full physical state.

  • Expected utility and the realized outcome

    Compare expected utilities under the stated objective. A larger outcome in one state need not mean larger expected utility.

  • The exact probability threshold

    Follow utility lines on fixed axes. Their crossing separates the regions where each action is optimal.

  • Identical percept, incompatible history-dependent optima

    Identical current observations can conceal different histories that require different optimal actions.

  • Hidden states can share the same best action

    Compare the objective assigned to each participant. Common interest and conflicting interest imply different decisions.

  • Bayes update: joint mass before normalization

    Evidence changes posterior weights. Distinguish the probability of the evidence from the posterior conditional on it.

  • A signal-contingent decision tree

    Follow each information branch, optimize within that branch, then average. Information cost is subtracted last.

  • Two local cleans and one necessary move

    Follow robot position, dirt state and accumulated action cost. Movement and cleaning alter different state components.

  • Belief propagation without a sensor

    An action updates the set of states still consistent with uncertainty. This set is not one actual world.

  • A key bit repairs an invalid state abstraction

    The chosen state representation must include information needed to decide legal actions, such as possession of a key.

  • Different paths produce different search nodes

    A search node carries a path, depth and cost; multiple nodes may represent the same state.

  • A self-loop generates infinitely many prefixes

    Different search histories can revisit the same physical state. An unbounded history tree can arise from a finite state graph.

  • Discounted return changes the preferred action

    Changing the discount changes the value of later rewards. The displayed order follows the actual discounted returns.

  • An inductive winning policy executed on actual counters

    Follow legal removals, whose turn it is and the remaining counters. A legal path alone is not an optimal strategy proof.

  • PEAS keeps sensing and acting separate

    Read performance, environment, actuators and sensors as different parts of one task specification.

  • Learning changes a component, not just a data counter

    Follow the selected learning-agent component and its actual input/output links; the critic does not choose the external action.

  • Regret compares against the best in each state

    Regret is relative to the best action in each state. The minimax action minimizes its largest statewise regret.
